_about: Typographica — the bibliographical apparatus of Tycho Brahe's printed works. One entry per Nielsen-style record (21: Tycho's own works surviving in print, the lost and the conjectured printings, the two works by others from his press, and one poem never printed); the editions and issues are the thesaurus manifestations joined by thesaurus_work; the copies are read from the census stores at build time and never stored here. Edition 2.0 (2026-09-05): the scholarly-edition rebuild — see _apply_2026-09-05_typographica_edition.py for every correction and its authority.

periods.title: I · Before the private press
periods.subtitle: Copenhagen jobbing printers, 1572–1573
periods.blurb: Tycho's first two publications were set by established Copenhagen printers: Mads Vingaard (the broadsheet elegy on his twin brother) and Lorentz Benedicht (the epoch-making De nova stella). He did not yet own a press.

periods.title: II · The Uraniborg private press
periods.subtitle: Hven, 1584–1597
periods.blurb: From 1584 Tycho ran his own press in a dedicated building south of Uraniborg, staffed by three printers known by name — Joachim, then Christopher Weida, then Hans Gaschitz, each in his service only briefly and otherwise unattested — Weida and Gaschitz probably Germans in Nielsen's judgement, Joachim of unrecorded origin — and supplied with type brokered through Rostock. It produced occasional poems to keep the printer busy between the great books — De mundi (1588), Epistolae (1596), the unfinished Progymnasmata (1592) — and the instrument-image broadsides (Icones). Several small prints survive in a single copy; four printings are known only from documents; one elegy of 1584, recovered in 1962 from a later reprint, is attributed to the press by conjecture.

periods.title: III · Wandsbek — the hybrid press
periods.subtitle: Rantzau's castle near Hamburg, 1597–1598
periods.blurb: Exiled from Hven, Tycho printed his masterpiece of self-presentation, the Mechanica, as a guest of Henrik Rantzau. Its colophon is only partly misleading. The press really was Tycho's, carried from Hven, and the colophon names its printer on its face — 'opera Philippi de Ohr Chalcographi Hamburgensis'. But Nielsen showed typographically that the type, the initials, and the flower-borders (Røskener) were all de Ohr's Hamburg stock: of Tycho's own material only the instrument-woodblocks and his printer's marks are in the book. A genuinely hybrid object, then, not a disguised one.

periods.title: IV · Posthumous completions & re-issues
periods.subtitle: Prague, Nuremberg, Frankfurt, 1602–1610
periods.blurb: After Tycho's death (24 Oct 1601) Kepler oversaw completion of the Progymnasmata (Prague, Schumann press, 1602) and a re-issue of De mundi (1603). The remaining stock passed to the booksellers Levinus Hülsius (Nuremberg, 1602) and then Gottfried Tampach (Frankfurt, 1610), who put the old Uraniborg sheets out afresh under new title-leaves. The Mechanica was the exception: Tengnagel sold its woodblocks to Hülsius, and Christoph Lochner reset the whole book in new type (Nuremberg 1602 = Norman 320) — a reprint, not a re-issue, and one still catalogued as '1598' wherever its title-leaf is lost.

sections.html: Tycho's plan was a vast work, a Theatrum astronomicum embracing the whole new astronomy. A press of his own answered several needs at once: the Copenhagen printers were busy and the city was plague-ridden; Hven's isolation made constant traffic with the mainland awkward; and he wished to guard his discoveries from those who might publish them as their own, and to oversee the setting and correction of his books sheet by sheet. The first notice of the press is his letter to Anders Sørensen Vedel of 16 February 1584, announcing that he would set up a small printing house on Uraniborg and procure type at the coming Frankfurt fair.

Tycho engaged a printer named Joachim and sent him to Wittenberg for presses and type; further type was brokered through his old Rostock teacher Heinrich Brucæus and the Rostock printer Stephan Möllmann ('Myliander') in 1584–85. The press was housed in a small building beside the castle — Tycho's own bird's-eye woodcut of Uraniborg marks the printing-house in the left-hand pavilion. Three printers are known by name: Joachim, then Christopher Weida (named in the 1588 colophon), then Hans Gaschitz (named in 1591). Nielsen records no nationality for Joachim; Weida and Gaschitz he judged probably Germans — all three otherwise unattested, and each apparently in Tycho's service only briefly.

Nielsen's analysis of the type and ornament stock is the means of telling a genuine Uraniborg imprint from later re-issues and imitations:
  • Roman (Antikva) — a Mittel (20 lines ≈ 114 mm), the commonest body-type; an exceptionally large Tekst-Antikva (10 lines ≈ 66 mm), the largest roman body-type used anywhere in 16th-century Denmark; and a Cicero (20 lines ≈ 94 mm) in two cuts (an older, fuller and a younger, slimmer).
  • Italic (Kursiv) — a large lille Tekst (10 lines ≈ 64 mm) and an old-style lille Cicero (20 lines ≈ 84 mm) with roman capitals, used for notes and small matter.
  • Fraktur — only two (a Cicero body ≈ 93 mm and a Tekst display ≈ 74 mm), and used only from 1591; no Schwabacher at all.
Twelve type-sets in all — the eight founts above, together with the capitals-only roman display founts Nielsen counts in with them. For ornament Tycho had just two sets of roman initials (shaded-foliage contour letters in the 'Spanish' style, ≈ 18 mm and ≈ 25 mm) and four vignettes. He never used title-frames, friezes, or flower-borders (Røskener) — which is why the rich flower-border decoration on every page of the 1598 Mechanica betrays it as Hamburg work, not Hven.

Paper was a constant difficulty. Tycho bought it at the Frankfurt fairs and sought it from princely mills (Henrik Rantzau's, and the Duke of Mecklenburg's, approached through his kinsman Heinrich v. Below in December 1587). To free himself of the shortage he built his own paper-mill on Hven, working by 1589 or 1590; its paper is recognisable by its two watermarks and its visibly lower quality — where a book passes from imported to island paper, the impression is markedly poorer. Nordstrand's study of the moulds identifies the mark itself: the Brahe arms — shield and helm, the crest of buffalo horns (Danish vesselhorn) set with peacock feathers, the letters T and B at the sides — recognised, among other sheets, in the observation protocol now KB GKS 317 2°. The watermarked island paper runs c. 1591–1597, which makes it a positive authentication mark for the Uraniborg books: the 1588 De mundi predates the mill, and the 1598 Wandsbek Mechanica — printed on the mainland with Hven paper fetched from store — falls outside the series. The oldest of the marks appears in sheets of the unfinished Progymnasmata (1592, completed 1602 from the 1592 stock).

Two woodcut marks carved at Uraniborg recur in the books: 'Astronomy', with the motto SVSPICIENDO DESPICIO ('looking up, I look down'), and 'Chemistry', with DESPICIENDO SVSPICIO ('looking down, I look up') — the allegorical figures that stood on the castle façade.

Tycho left Hven on 29 March 1597 (Nielsen gives 29 April; the date adopted here is the Loca register's, from Tycho's own statement), taking press and instruments with him. The Mechanica was printed at Wandsbek near Hamburg in 1598 on a hybrid press (his own, but with the Hamburg printer Philip de Ohr's type and ornament); an attempt to print the Progymnasmata Moon-section at Hamburg was so botched that the whole run was scrapped; a further attempt at Wittenberg (winter 1598–99, on Hven paper fetched from the Wandsbek store) was abandoned for Prague. The press reached Prague in 1600.

After Tycho's death Kepler saw the Progymnasmata through the Prague Schumann press (1602); the remaining stock passed to Levinus Hülsius at Nuremberg (1602; the Mechanica reprinted by Christoph Lochner) and then to Gottfried Tampach at Frankfurt (1610). Only with the 1610 Tampach re-issues was the original Uraniborg stock finally exhausted; when a wholly new edition of the works appeared at Frankfurt in 1648, it was new printing from first to last.

entries.gloss: A Latin elegy on Tycho's stillborn twin brother — his first appearance in print, and the true beginning of the corpus.

This is the work that established Tycho's reputation and overturned the Aristotelian dogma of celestial immutability.

entries.survival: One copy located — the Royal Danish Library, Copenhagen; Nielsen 1931 records no other holding.

entries.production: Among the first prints run off the new press in late 1584, set to test its capacity and to keep the printer occupied; its type matches the later Uraniborg books.
entries.note_html: The earliest known Uraniborg imprint. A long-promised tribute to Johannes Pratensis (professor of medicine at Copenhagen, d. 1576), now redeemed once Tycho's new press could set it. The colophon misprints the place 'Vranibutgi' (t for r); Nielsen marks it [!].

entries.note_html: Tycho says in the poem itself that he had it printed in part to keep his new press occupied. It is the internal evidence that fixes the lost Gjøe and Lange poems to the same season (late 1584).

entries.production: The two woodblocks were reused in Tycho's later books. Writing to Hagecius on 25 August 1585 he explained that his woodcutter had gone to Germany, so only these two instrument-blocks were yet cut; the rest would follow on the man's return.
entries.note_html: Why it survives only at Marburg. This broadside is a printed enclosure to Tycho's autograph letter to Landgrave Wilhelm IV of Hesse-Kassel (1 March 1586, received Kassel 10 April), bound into the Kassel-retained correspondence convolute now HStAM Best. 3 II, Nr. 1070 (former 4a.31.14). Mentioned in Tycho's letter to Hagecius (25 August 1585): more instrument prints would follow once the woodcutter returned from Germany. Nielsen gives it its own entry, 976, separate from the c. 1596 Icones album (975): the first stage of the same enterprise, eleven years earlier, and entered here separately as he enters it.

entries.survival: Two title-page settings: the earlier, rejected setting — whose title reads De novis aetherei mundi generationibus … and whose preface is set differently — survives in the Berlin copy alone; every other copy carries the definitive title. Most of the edition was held back to be issued with the first volume and reached the market only in the Prague re-issue of 1603 (Nielsen 1921, p. 211).

entries.production: Printing of the great work began with this volume, before vol. I. Through chronic paper shortages — in December 1587 Tycho sought paper from the Duke of Mecklenburg's mills through his kinsman Heinrich v. Below — it was finished on 8 March 1588, the day the Uraniborg weather-diary records 'Finis I lib'.
entries.note_html: The colophon naming Christopher Weida is the only Tycho imprint to name him. The text was finished 8 March 1588 ('Finis I lib' in the Uraniborg meteorological diary). Two title-page settings exist: the standard one (10 chapters per the preface) and an earlier, rejected setting (titled De novis aetherei mundi generationibus, 8 chapters), known only from one Berlin Staatsbibliothek copy. Re-issued posthumously at Prague (Schumann, 1603) and Frankfurt (Tampach, 1610); most surviving 'Liber II' copies are in fact 1588 sheets in later bindings.

entries.gloss: An album of 18 woodcut instrument-images — the immediate predecessor of the Mechanica, sent as a supplement to the Epistolae.
entries.survival: Nielsen knew three copies (Wrocław, Stockholm, Vienna). A fourth, in an Epistolae + Icones sammelband recorded in Thesaurus Librorum Danicorum 257, passed from Lindskoug (Malmö) through the Lindskoug sale of 1937 to Bruun Rasmussen in 2022 (sale 908, lot 176) and is in the trade. The Vienna copy is a distinct issue: its title-leaf is reset and a printed afterword added, neither printed at Uraniborg.

entries.production: Eighteen instrument-woodcuts assembled as a supplement to the Epistolae, printed one to a page with no captions. Nielsen's typographic analysis shows the Vienna copy's reset title-leaf and printed afterword were not printed at Uraniborg — most likely by Philip de Ohr at Hamburg in early 1598, when Tycho was at Wandsbek.
entries.note_html: The Icones was sent as a supplement to the Epistolae (1596), whose bound-in instrument descriptions supply the captions these plates lack. The Vienna afterword announces the forthcoming Mechanica: the Icones is thus the immediate predecessor of the 1598 masterpiece.

entries.production: Long in the press: as early as 1590 Tycho's pupil Gellius Sascerides handed the printed sheet G — carrying important star observations — to Magini in Bologna. By 1590 two presses ran at Uraniborg at once, one on the Progymnasmata and one on this correspondence. Quires LL and MM (pp. 265–80) exist in two settings; the Gheyn copper-portrait was cut c. 1590, probably for this book.
entries.note_html: Dedicated to the young Landgrave Moritz (successor to Wilhelm IV), the volume prints Tycho's correspondence with Wilhelm IV and the Kassel astronomer Christopher Rothmann, with a German-and-Latin description of Uraniborg and Stjerneborg and new woodcut views. The autograph originals survive in the Kassel-retained convolute HStAM Best. 3 II, Nr. 1070 (former 4a.31.14) at Marburg — several letters holograph — and Tycho cut and revised the letters for print, making the convolute the primary collation source against this edition. Re-issued by Hülsius (Nuremberg 1602, new title-leaf only) and Tampach (Frankfurt 1610).

entries.gloss: Volume I of Tycho's restoration of astronomy — begun at Uraniborg in 1592, printed-but-unfinished, completed posthumously at Prague in 1602.
entries.survival: Of the Uraniborg printing itself no copy is located: the Berlin copy (partial) and the Marburg title-leaf fragment are recorded but await re-verification, and Tycho's own working copy — given to Johannes Müller in March 1598, last at Königsberg — has been untraced since 1944–45. Every located copy is of the Prague completion of 1602, entered below, whose census includes the copies dated 1603 on the title. Quires M and DDDD of the Uraniborg printing exist in two settings.

B, p. 9) Caput Primum on the solar course. The text breaks off unfinished — the Moon section (quires P–R) was never printed at Uraniborg.

entries.production: Printed by the lacuna method: unfinished sections were skipped, a fixed run of sheets left blank, and printing carried on — so the book was years in the press and finished only after Tycho's death. The 1592 collective title-leaf went out as advance copies (3 to the Landgrave of Hesse on 20 Feb, 3 to Hugo Blotius on 20 Mar, 6 to Hagecius on 22 Mar 1592). The Königsberg copy — Tycho's own working copy, given to the assistant Johannes Müller in March 1598, with twelve blank leaves bound where the Moon-section was pending and his autograph corrections throughout — showed exactly what was printed on Hven against what was completed at Prague; it has been untraced since the dispersal of the Königsberg collections in 1944–45, and is known now only from Nielsen's description (§433).
entries.note_html: The 1592 title-leaf was an advance/collective title; Tycho sent advance copies (collective title + portrait + Rudolf II's privilege) to scholarly contacts, and three went to the Landgrave of Hesse in February 1592; of that consignment what survives at Marburg is a single title-leaf fragment. Completed posthumously at the Schumann press (Prague 1602) under Kepler's oversight; re-issued by Tampach (Frankfurt 1610) with quires B, C, Kk and Ll reset in many copies.
scripta: the prolegomena on the sun and moon

entries.gloss: Tycho's illustrated catalogue of his instruments and of Uraniborg itself — the masterpiece of scientific self-presentation, dedicated to Rudolf II.
entries.survival: The first edition; the Nuremberg reprint of 1602 is entered as its own edition below. Most copies are illuminated and carry de Gheyn's engraved portrait pasted to the title-verso; a large group are presentation copies with Tycho's autograph dedication (the surviving copies, below). Hasselberg listed thirty-three copies in 1904, Nielsen added two.

H) the appendix on the architecture of the observatory; Bl. 42b the colophon: 'IMPRESSVM WANDESBVRGI IN ARCE RANZOVIANA … PROPRIA AVTHORIS TYPOGRAPHIA opera Philippi de Ohr Chalcographi Hamburgensis Ineunte ANNO M.D.IIC.' In most copies a portrait of Tycho is pasted onto Bl. 1b.

entries.production: Printed at Wandsbek early in 1598 by the Hamburg printer Philip de Ohr (who from 1597 used the Binder family's material). Nielsen's type-analysis shows the body-type, initials, friezes, vignettes and flower-borders are de Ohr's or Binder's; of Tycho's own material only the instrument-woodblocks and his printer's marks are in the book — the press itself, however, was his, carried from Hven. Hasselberg's census (Vierteljahrsschrift der Astronomischen Gesellschaft 39, 1904) lists 33 copies, to which Nielsen added two more, at Danzig and Kiel; most of the surviving copies are illuminated, and most have Gheyn's engraved portrait pasted onto the title-verso.
entries.note_html: Dedicated to Rudolf II, dated 31 December 1597. 18 of the 22 instrument-plates are printed from the existing Uraniborg woodblocks; the 4 new ones (including the great mural quadrant with Tycho's portrait, and the great celestial globe) are copperplate engravings cut in Germany. The colophon's propria authoris typographia is true as far as it goes — the press was Tycho's own — and it names Philip de Ohr on its face; what it obscures is how much of the finished book is Hamburg work. Re-issued as a complete new reprint by Hülsius (Nuremberg 1602, printed by Christoph Lochner; = Norman 320), which is catalogued as '1598' where its title-leaf is lost.

epistolarium.label: The attesting letter — Tycho → Rothmann, 17 August 1588 (confirms it was 'written four years ago')

entries.gloss: A lost printed poem to Falk Gjøe — attested only by a correspondent who received a copy at the Frankfurt fair.
entries.survival: No copy survives.
entries.note_html: Known only from Christoffer Rothmann's letter of 21 September 1587, describing the printed leaves he received at the Frankfurt fair from Hans Aalborg, with two emblem-woodcuts on the verso. Tycho's reply (17 August 1588) confirms it was 'written four years ago' (i.e. late 1584), and the surviving Ulfeldt poem (LN 426) names it as a companion piece.

entries.gloss: A lost printed poem to Erik Lange, the alchemist who would marry Tycho's sister Sophie; the text survives in manuscript.
entries.survival: No printed copy survives. The text survives in manuscript and was first printed in the Opera Omnia, vol. XV (1929), p. 6, where Dreyer notes that this poem too appears to have been printed at Tycho's press and that every printed copy perished.
entries.note_html: Named, together with the Gjøe poem, in the surviving Carmen ad Ulfeldium (LN 426) as a companion piece sent the same season (late 1584). Erik Lange later married Tycho's sister Sophie Brahe. No copy survives.

entries.gloss: A lost elegy on the physician-poet Hans Frandsen (Johannes Franciscus Ripensis), known only through later reprints.
entries.survival: No print copy survives; the text is preserved by Gassendi (1655) and Resen (1668).
entries.note_html: Tycho's elegy on Hans Frandsen / Johannes Franciscus Ripensis, professor of medicine at Copenhagen, who died 4 July 1584. The text was reprinted by Gassendi, Tychonis Brahei vita (1655) pp. 261–62, and by Resen, Inscriptiones Hafnienses (1668) pp. 83–84 — but no copy of the original Uraniborg printing is known. (Frandsen had himself contributed the opening poem to Tycho's De nova stella, LN 429.)

entries.gloss: An elegy in praise of Claudius Ptolemy, dated 1 October 1584, attributed to the Uraniborg press by conjecture: no printing is attested, and the text is known only from a 1644 reprint recovered in 1962.
entries.survival: No Uraniborg printing is attested. The text survives in a single witness, the last leaf of G. L. Frobenius's 1644 Almagest proof-sheet at Kungliga biblioteket, Stockholm (a microfilm at the Royal Danish Library).
entries.collation: 16 elegiac distichs (32 lines), composed as a verse inscription to stand beneath a portrait of Ptolemy. The original Uraniborg setting (if it was printed there) is described in no source; only Frobenius's 1644 single-page reprint is known.
entries.contents: An elegy 'on the likeness of Claudius Ptolemy', dated 1 October 1584, setting Ptolemy's bloodless intellectual conquest of earth and heaven against the bloody, partial conquests of Rome. Brøndsted reads it as one of the occasional poems Tycho printed in autumn–winter 1584–85 to advertise his new Uraniborg press (cf. the lost Gjøe and Lange pieces); Frobenius's 1644 print is an ‘eftertryk’ (reprint) detached from its original portrait context.
entries.references: First published, with facsimile (p. 73): Mogens Brøndsted, 'Et ukendt digt af Tycho Brahe', ‘Fund og Forskning’ 9 (1962), 71–78. Not in Dreyer's ‘Opera Omnia’ — a 20th-century addition to the Tycho corpus.
entries.nielsen_census: No Nielsen number — unknown to Nielsen 1931, recovered 1962. Sole witness: Stockholm, Kungliga biblioteket (the Frobenius 1644 ‘Almagest’ proof-sheet; Brøndsted gives no precise shelfmark). Stockholm survival probably via Jørgen Seefeld's library and the 1645 Swedish war-loot.
entries.note_html: Recovered 1962. A hitherto-unknown Latin elegy by Tycho on a portrait of Claudius Ptolemy, headed 'In effigiem Cl. Ptolemæi Alexandrini. Elegia Tychonis Brahe, scripta A.C. 1584. Kal. VIIIbr.' Mogens Brøndsted found it on the last leaf of Georg Ludwig Frobenius's folio proof-sheet for a planned new Latin Almagest (Hamburg, 1644) — the same Frobenius who had spent six weeks in Tycho's familia on Hven in 1591 (see the Bibliotheca; the same scholar's printer's-manuscript is KB GKS 320). The 1584 date places the poem beside the occasional pieces Tycho printed to occupy his new press, and on that parallel alone a Uraniborg printing has been conjectured: nothing attests it, and the elegy survives only because Frobenius printed it sixty years later.
entries.text_witness_heading: IN EFFIGIEM CL. PTOLEMÆI | ALEXANDRINI. | Elegia Tychonis Brahe, scripta A.C. 1584. Kal. VIIIbr. | (H)ic oculos, faciem, barbam, sic membra gerebat / Claudius, is nomen cui Ptolemæus erat. | … |
entries.title_full: In effigiem Cl. Ptolemæi Alexandrini, elegia

epistolarium.label: The attesting letter — Tycho → Bartholomäus Scultetus, 7 January 1600 (confirms the Hamburg printing)

entries.gloss: Tycho's lost reply to the Scotsman John Craig on the parallax of comets — printed, fiercely defended as printed, but vanished.
entries.survival: No printed copy of either printing is located. The text survives in manuscript: Copenhagen, Royal Danish Library, NKS 93b 2° (the base manuscript of the Opera Omnia edition); a Berlin fragment apparently copied from the print and prefaced by Craig's three letters; and untraced copies among the Kepler papers and in the Longomontanus–From line.
entries.production: Printed at Uraniborg in 1591, then — enlarged — at Wandsbek/Hamburg in 1598 (the latter from Tycho's letter to Scultetus, 7 Jan 1600). Craig's longer rebuttal reached Tycho only in May 1592, after the first printing, prompting the reissue; a further, unfinished refutation was left in manuscript at his death.
entries.note_html: The most contested of the lost prints. Tycho's Apologetica responsio answered John Craig's three critical letters on the 1588 De mundi. Friis and Dreyer both doubted a printed edition ever existed, following Gassendi's claim that it survived only in Longomontanus's manuscript. But Rasmus Bartholin, in De cometis (1665) p. 49, states flatly that he owns a printed copy ('quam impressam habeo Uraniburgi 1591'), expressly to refute Gassendi. So: printed at Uraniborg 1591, then enlarged and reprinted at Wandsbek/Hamburg 1598 (the latter confirmed by Tycho's own letter to Scultetus, 7 Jan 1600), all copies dispersed by the mid-17th century. A fragmentary manuscript in Berlin appears to be copied from the printed edition; Copenhagen holds NKS 93b. Both printings are entered in the census register; no copy of either is known.

printings_evidence.evidence: Rasmus Bartholin, De cometis (1665), p. 49: 'quam impressam habeo Uraniburgi 1591', said expressly against Gassendi's claim that the work survived only in Longomontanus's manuscript; the Berlin fragment copied from the print. Friis and Dreyer had followed Gassendi in doubting a print; Nielsen's verdict (1921, pp. 194–195) is that it was printed.

Tycho to Bartholomaeus Scultetus, Prague, 7 January 1600: the defensive writings 'have indeed been printed at Hamburg' but are to be printed anew with a further refutation; Houzeau and Lancaster, Bibliographie générale de l'astronomie I.1, col. 599, list '[Wandesburgi] 1598' without a stated source. Nielsen (1921, p. 207): 'the matter is not entirely clear'.

entries.title_full: Apologetica responsio ad cujusdam Peripatetici in Scotia dubia, sibi de parallaxi cometarum opposita

entries.gloss: The earliest graphic representation of Uraniborg — three woodcut views with Latin descriptions, sent with the Rantzau poem.
entries.survival: Unicum — the Hessisches Staatsarchiv, Marburg.

[Under each woodcut a detailed Latin explanation.]
entries.collation: Single leaf, patent (broadsheet), transverse. Type-area of the whole leaf: 290 × 357 mm. Italic. Three woodcuts above three columns of Latin text (DB 1220).
entries.contents: A left-hand elevation of the castle seen from the east (PRÆCIPVÆ ET MAIORIS DOMVS DELINEATIO); a right-hand bird's-eye view of the castle and its surroundings (TOTIVS AMBITVS ET CAPACITATIS DELINEATIO); and, centred below, a ground-plan (ICHNOGRAPHIA PRÆCIPVÆ DOMVS) — each over a column of explanatory Latin keyed by letters to the views.
entries.production: One of the small prints finished early in 1585; first mentioned in the Rantzau poem of 1 March 1585. The bird's-eye view shows the ramparts before their four corner bastions were added — the form by which Nielsen recognised it as the original of Braun's later engraving. The surviving copy reached the Landgrave of Hesse as an enclosure to Tycho's letter of 1 March 1586.

entries.note_html: The earliest known image of Uraniborg, and the source of the engraving in Braun's Theatrum urbium (Cologne 1586). It survives only at Marburg, as a printed enclosure to Tycho's correspondence with Landgrave Wilhelm IV of Hesse-Kassel, bound together with the LN 976 instrument broadside.
entries.nielsen_note: Entered in the Dansk Bibliografi under its title (p. 415, no. 1220) and cross-referenced from the Brahe section (p. 63), exactly as the two Icones are.

entries.gloss: The first true book from the Uraniborg press — an astrological-meteorological almanac for 1586, by Tycho's assistant Elias Olsen Morsing under Tycho's imprimatur.
entries.survival: The Royal Danish Library holds three copies, one with Tycho's autograph dedication to the Schleswig pastor Albert Meier (Nielsen 1921, p. 187); Nielsen's 1931 list names some eighteen libraries, and the almanac is not rare.

Gr. Latitudinem. 56. Gr. | Excusum in Officina VRANIBVRGICA. |

entries.contents: Bl. 1a title; 1b blank; Bl. 2–4 the author's dedication to Crown Prince Christian (later Christian IV), dated 1 January 1586; Bl. 5–6a preface; Bl. 6b the treatise 'De cometa seu stella crinita rotunda' on the comet first seen 18 October 1585; Bl. 17a the diary proper; Bl. 17b–29a astronomical tables; Bl. 29b the press's emblem with its motto; Bl. 30a the colophon 'IMPRESSVM VRANIBVRGI IN INSVLA CELEBRIS PORTHMI DANICI HVÆNA.'
entries.production: Planned as six quaterns in 2,000 copies (Tycho's letter of 8 January 1585; the run actually printed is not attested), on imported paper (the island paper-mill did not yet exist). The signing — Aa–Dd before A–D — shows the calendar section (the last 14 leaves) was set first, in late 1585; the front matter followed early in 1586. The almanac was enlarged with the treatise on the round, tail-less comet observed on Hven in October–November 1585. One Copenhagen copy has a leaf bearing Tycho's autograph dedication to the Schleswig pastor Albert Meier.

entries.note_html: By Tycho's assistant Elias Olsen Morsing, printed 'in Officina VRANIBVRGICA' and dedicated to the not-quite-nine-year-old Crown Prince Christian (later Christian IV). It bears Tycho's 'Astronomy' emblem with the motto SVSPICIENDO DESPICIO. The first genuine book — as opposed to broadsheet — to issue from the press. Nielsen number LN 1170.

entries.gloss: Peder Jacobsen Flemløs's elemental-and-terrestrial astrology — the only Danish-language book ever printed at Uraniborg (with a parallel German edition).
entries.survival: Both the Danish (LN 606) and German (LN 607) editions are rare; no Scandinavian copy of the German edition survives.

B) Part I, ch. 1 ('Tegen til tørt oc klart Værligt aff Solen' — signs of dry and clear weather from the Sun); Bl. 63b–80a registers and errata; colophon 'Tryct paa Vraniborg CVM PRIVILEGIO. Aff Hans Gaschitz Bogprenter sammesteds Anno 1591. Mense Junie.'
entries.production: Printed by Hans Gaschitz — like Weida, a German otherwise unattested who served only briefly. The Danish setting (LN 606) left the press in June 1591; the German edition (LN 607, 'Eine elementische und irdische Astrologia'), of identical format and extent but with richer ornament, followed in September 1591.
entries.nielsen_census: Danish (LN 606): Karlsruhe (Landesbibl.); *Copenhagen, Kgl. Bibl., Univ. Bibl.; Oslo (Univ. Bibl., defective). German (LN 607): Groningen; Karlsruhe; *Vienna (Bibl. d. techn. Hochschule).
entries.references: F. R. Friis's reprint of the original (Copenhagen 1865). F. Magnússen, in Annaler f. nord. Oldkyndighed 1840–41, 326–31; Friis, Ped. Jakobsen Flemløs, 5–7; L. Nielsen, in Nord. tidskr. VIII, 192–93.
entries.note_html: Written by Peder Jacobsen Flemløs (Tycho's assistant 1578–88) at the request of Frederik II, who wanted an account of the signs of coming weather; the preface — composed in Flemløs's name by Longomontanus — records that Tycho had it printed to keep his printer occupied while paper was being readied for the great astronomical work. The only Danish-language book from the Uraniborg press, and its first use of Fraktur. The earlier Ægloga by Flemløs on the November 1574 solar eclipse (Copenhagen, 1574) is censused separately — see its census.
scripta: the preface written in Flemløs's name

entries.gloss: Tycho's most ambitious poem — 608 lines in elegiac couplets, in Sophie Brahe's voice to Erik Lange, never printed in his lifetime and the primary evidence for Tycho as a humanist-literary figure.
entries.survival: Two manuscript witnesses: V = Cod. Vindob. Lat. 10686/12 (ÖNB Vienna; item 12 per Friis's 1868 inventory); R = Resen, Inscriptiones Hafnienses (Copenhagen, 1668). V is primary, with corrections in two hands — T (Tycho's autograph) and X (unknown). No independent printed edition in Tycho's lifetime.
entries.diplomatic: [Inedita — no printed title-page. Published as:] URANIA TITANI | in Tychonis Brahe Opera Omnia, vol. IX (Dreyer ed., 1922), pp. 193–230.
entries.collation: 608 lines in elegiac couplets: the heroide proper is exactly 600 verses (Zeeberg 1994, comm. ad v. 1 — the ‘sexcentos … versus’ of the opening line, read as deliberate number-symbolism), framed by a 4-line verse address and a 4-line subscription (vv. 605–8). Transmitted by one primary MS (Cod. Vindob. Lat. 10686/12) and a 17th-c. printed text (Resen 1668). Not independently printed in Tycho's lifetime. First partial edition: F. R. Friis, Danske Samlinger IV (1868–69). Standard text: TBOO IX, pp. 193–230.
entries.contents: A verse epistle (Ovidian heroide) written in Sophie Brahe's voice to her absent beloved Erik Lange, with Tycho himself appearing under the pseudonym Apollo. Urania = Sophie Brahe; Titan = Erik Lange; Apollo = Tycho Brahe. Composed at Uraniborg in winter 1594 when Lange had been abroad for years in pursuit of the philosopher's stone. The poem is layered with alchemical and astrological imagery and closes with four embedded horoscopes (for Titan/Lange, Urania/Sophie Brahe, Tage Thott, and Apollo/Tycho) reconstructed by Ove von Späth in Zeeberg's 1994 edition.
entries.references: T. Brahe, Opera omnia IX, pp. 193–230 (ed. Dreyer, 1922). F. R. Friis, Danske Samlinger IV (1868–69), pp. 1–13 (partial; from Friis's 1868 inventory of Cod. Vindob. Lat. 10686). P. Zeeberg, Tycho Brahes »Urania Titani«: Et digt om Sophie Brahe, Renæssancestudier 7 (Copenhagen: Museum Tusculanum, 1994), 320 pp. — first critical edition with complete Danish translation, literary commentary, and the Ove von Späth horoscope reconstructions.
entries.nielsen_census: No Nielsen number — inedita. Primary MS: Vienna, ÖNB, Cod. Vindob. Lat. 10686/12. Secondary printed text: Resen, Inscriptiones Hafnienses (Copenhagen, 1668). No census of print copies; the 1584 printed poem to Erik Lange has its own entry.
entries.production: Composed at Uraniborg in winter 1594, before 26 July 1594 — the date of Tycho's covering letter to the Scottish jurist Thomas Craig (TBOO VII.366), which encloses the poem as ‘sororis nomine a me lusam’. Tycho's authorship has been the standard scholarly view since Zeeberg 1994, grounded in Tycho's own claim in that letter, though a minority attribution to Jon Jacobsen Venusin — Gellius Sascerides's brother-in-law, not Gellius himself — is argued in Andersen-Vinilandicus (2009), pp. 225–276, and remains an open question. The Vienna MS (V) carries two layers of autograph correction — hand T (identified as Tycho's) and hand X (unknown) — establishing Tycho's direct involvement with the text regardless of primary authorship.
entries.note_html: Tycho's literary magnum opus. At 608 lines in elegiac couplets, Urania Titani is his longest poem — a sustained Ovidian heroide written in Sophie Brahe's voice to her absent beloved Erik Lange, with Tycho appearing as the god Apollo. Written in winter 1594 at Uraniborg, it is the richest surviving window onto the intellectual interior of the island: alchemical longing, astrological symbolism, and the intimate pseudonym-world of the Brahe circle all run through it. Its four embedded horoscopes — of Erik Lange, of Sophie Brahe, of the young Tage Thott, and of Tycho himself, who casts his own nativity in his sister's voice — were reconstructed from the verse by Ove von Späth for Zeeberg's 1994 edition; all four are in Horoscopi. Tycho claims the poem as his own: sending it to the Scottish jurist Thomas Craig on 26 July 1594 he encloses an Epistola Elegiaca ad imitationem Ovidianarum … sororis nomine a me lusam — an elegiac epistle in Ovid's manner, composed by me in my sister's name (TBOO VII.366) — and it is this first-person attestation on which Zeeberg's attribution rests. A minority ascription to Jon Jacobsen Venusin (Andersen-Vinilandicus 2009) remains open. First published in full by Dreyer (TBOO IX, 1922); first critically edited and translated into Danish by Peter Zeeberg (Museum Tusculanum, 1994) — the monograph that opened Tycho Brahe studies as a branch of Danish literary history (Receptio, 1994).
entries.title_full: Urania Titani — Urania (Sophie Brahe) to Titan (Erik Lange)

opus._about: The never-realised grand work — the Theatri Astronomici Opus — that was the end goal of Tycho's whole printing programme. Reconstructed from the primary documents read verbatim (the 1592 Quaternio Primus, the Peucer letter of 13 September 1588, the Mechanica) and the biographies given in the Sources.
opus.tagline: the work all the rest were fragments of
opus.intro: The printings gathered in this edition were never meant to stand alone. Tycho conceived his entire output as one branded restoration of astronomy (instauratio astronomiae) culminating in a single great work he named, in print and in his own hand, with the genitive formula “Theatri Astronomici Opus” — the Work of the Astronomical Theatre. It was never assembled. What survives are the realized fragments — and the visible scars of the parts that never came.
opus.structure_note: The plan had two tiers: an introductory series on “recent phenomena” (the 1572 nova, the comets), explicitly a prodromus — the forerunner that “prepares the way” — and the systematic great work, which Tycho divided in his letter to Caspar Peucer of 13 September 1588 into seven books. The geo-heliocentric cosmology is not a topic inside the opus; it is the organizing principle of the book-division.

tier1.label: Tier 1 · The introductory series
tier1.gloss: “On the more recent phenomena of the aethereal world” — a preparatory trilogy, the forerunner to the great work.

slots.title: The new star of 1572
slots.detail: The nova — but already carrying the restored solar motion and the fixed-star certification. In expanding it swallowed systematic Books III–IV.

slots.title: The comet of 1577, with the world-system
slots.detail: The Tychonic system + an Apologia. Its own title-page calls it Liber Secundus — a Book Two whose Books One and Three never came as planned.

slots.title: The later comets
slots.detail: Three (then four) further comets — 1580, 1582, 1585, [1590]. Printing was reported begun in February 1590, but how much was printed is unknown and nothing of it survives (Nielsen 1921, p. 199). What Tycho wrote — chiefly his material on the comet of 1585 — Dreyer edited in the Opera Omnia (TBOO IV); the comet observations themselves fill TBOO XIII.

tier2.label: Tier 2 · The seven-book systematic work
tier2.gloss: “I have resolved to distribute the Astronomical Work itself into seven books” — Tycho to Caspar Peucer, 13 September 1588.

source_link.text: The source — read Tycho's letter to Peucer, Hven, 13 September 1588

tier2.ancillary_note: Books I–II are ancillary by Tycho's own word (ceteris inservientia, “serving the rest”): instruments and trigonometry are the apparatus that makes the observational books possible, placed first as foundation.

books.title: Instruments / Mechanics
books.content: the fabric and use of his instruments

books.title: Trigonometry
books.content: the science of triangles and numbers; the computational shortcuts (prosthaphaeresis) that relieve “our predecessors' excessive labours”
books.status_label: a trigonometry manual survives in MS — identified here with Book II
books.ms: Triangulorum planorum et sphaericorum praxis arithmetica — a compendium of 7 plane + 9 spherical triangle-solving rules. Prague codex NK 14 C 20 (in a calligrapher's hand, not Tycho's); Studnička's 1886 facsimile (editio princeps); critical text: TBOO I, pp. 281–293 (1913), “quae vivo Tychone edita non est” (not published in Tycho's lifetime). DSL assigns 1591; surviving recension colophon 19 Nov 1595. Strano & Truffa call Book II “without equivalent among Tycho's works” — wrongly: a Tycho trigonometry treatise demonstrably survives, and its content answers the Peucer letter's Book II point for point (triangles, numbers, prosthaphaeretic compendia). The identification of this manuscript with the planned Book II is the editor's: no earlier author makes the equation, and Tycho nowhere states it. Existence certain (TBOO I); the identification defensible but unattested.

books.title: Fixed stars / the eighth sphere
books.content: the “exact verification” of the stellar sphere — the star catalogue
books.status_label: partial → 777 stars printed; 1004 only in manuscript

books.title: Sun & Moon
books.content: their circuits referred to a resting Earth — an upgraded solar model + a wholly new five-circle lunar theory (Tycho's “variation”)

books.title: Venus & Mercury
books.content: models for the two inferior planets, that circle the Sun but not also the Earth
books.status_label: never written — only the De mundi world-diagram

books.title: Mars, Jupiter & Saturn
books.content: models for the three superior planets, that encircling the Sun enclose the Earth
books.status_label: a Saturn model only; Mars left to Kepler

books.title: Latitudes of the five planets
books.status_label: never written — “no part can be found”

opus.tally: Of the seven: two realized (I, IV), two partial (III — 777 stars printed; VI — a Saturn model only), one answered by a surviving manuscript (II — an identification made here by the editor, unattested in the earlier literature), two never written (V, VII). The unified opus was never assembled.

privilege.intro: Tycho did not only plan the opus privately — he advertised it in print and secured imperial protection for it.
privilege.quaternio_note: The 1592 Quaternio Primus — the collective title-leaf and prospectus for the Progymnasmata — is the documentary keystone joining the two tiers: it declares the whole Progymnasmata to stand Prodromi loco (“in the place of a forerunner”) to the greater opus, and bound into it is Rudolf II's printing privilege. Nielsen (§433) knew three witnesses to the 1592 advance issue, and the census of it grades them: Berlin, Staatsbibliothek — a partial copy, extant, though its WW2 survival is still to be confirmed; Marburg, Hessisches Staatsarchiv — the title-leaf alone; and the Königsberg working copy — Tycho's own, corrected throughout in his hand, with twelve blank leaves bound in where the Moon section was still pending — which the census grades lost: the Königsberg collections were dispersed or destroyed in 1944–45 and no post-war trace has been found. It is the witness that mattered most, the one object that could have fixed the boundary between what was printed on Hveen and what was completed in Prague.

diploma.label: The Diploma Caesareum · 13 June 1590
diploma.source: Rudolf II to Tycho Brahe · signed by the Emperor, countersigned Curtius and Barvitius
diploma.description: Rudolf II granted a 30-year Empire-wide printing privilege. Its language defines the planned opus, by imperial authority, as the third world-system after Ptolemy and Copernicus:
diploma.quote: new hypotheses of the celestial motions, agreeing exactly with the observations of all ages — which was achieved neither by the earlier hypotheses of Ptolemy nor by the later ones of Copernicus
diploma.gloss: The opus was officially conceived as the restoration of astronomy that would supersede both predecessors — Tycho's own claim, ratified by the Emperor.

curtius.label: Jacobus Curtius to Tycho · 28 June 1590
curtius.source: Curtius drafted the privilege himself and later hosted Tycho in Prague. Fifteen days after the diploma he wrote:
curtius.quote: …ubi majus illud, quod moliris, Opus, in lucem prodierit. Neque enim dubito, quin … indeque novam hanc mundi Machinam, divino sane ingenio, extruxeris.
curtius.gloss: “…when that greater Work which you are building shall have come to light. Nor do I doubt that … from it you will have built up this new Machine of the world, by a truly divine genius.”

title_box.label: The name, settled

attestations.quote: … viam praeparant, ad maius illud THEATRI ASTRONOMICI OPVS, omnibus Mundi aetatibus sufficienter inserviturum
attestations.gloss: “… prepare the way to that greater Work of the Astronomical Theatre, destined to serve sufficiently all the ages of the world.”
“This fuller and universal exposition we reserve for the Work of the Astronomical Theatre.”

attestations.quote: Hoc nostrum Astronomicae redintegrationis Theatrum, quam primum solide et totaliter extructum absolutumque fuerit …
attestations.gloss: “this our Theatre of the restoration of Astronomy, as soon as it shall have been solidly and wholly built and completed…”

title_box.note: Tycho's own form is always the genitive. The tidy nominative “Theatrum astronomicum” is not his and not Gassendi's (whose 1655 Vita also prints the genitive) — it was fixed by Dreyer in 1890 and inherited by Nielsen, Norlind and Christianson. A contemporary, Magini, already called the masterwork a “Theatrum” (c. 1590).
title_box.disambig: Not to be confused with Longomontanus's Introductio in Theatrum Astronomicum (Copenhagen, 1639) — a different book by Tycho's former assistant, in which theatrum means the literal new Copenhagen observatory (the Round Tower). A 47-years-later coincidence of idiom.

evolution.label: A moving target
evolution.intro: The architecture was never fixed. The record preserves three successive states of it — 1588, 1592, 1598 — and across them Tycho twice re-cut the boundary between the “recent phenomena” volumes and the systematic books.

steps.desc: Peucer letter: a three-tome comet trilogy plus a separate seven-book systematic opus.
Quaternio Primus: the Progymnasmata is now “in three books” that fold planetary content into the introductory frame (superior planets in Book II, inferior in Book III).
Mechanica: re-cut again — all comets into volume II, all five planets into volume III.

tycho.label: Tycho’s timetable
tycho.source: Peucer letter · Uraniborg, 13 September 1588 · TBOO VII, p. 132
tycho.estimate_gloss: “within five or six years” — completion estimated c. 1593–94

bottlenecks.title: Computational
bottlenecks.text: New mean-motion and prosthaphaeresis tables had to be built afresh for each planet — precisely the labour the manuscript Triangulorum praxis (Book II) was meant to mechanize.

bottlenecks.title: Observational
bottlenecks.text: More acronychal observations of the superior planets were needed — “above all in Saturn, because of the slowness of its motion.”

tycho.sequence_note: He set a sequencing rule: issue first the material needing no long delay — “what is contained in the first four or five books” — and leave the planetary Books VI–VII, needing the most new observation, for last.

verdict.label: Beyond reach in principle
verdict.events: The five-year estimate was overtaken by events: loss of royal favour, departure from Hven on 29 April 1597, years in exile, and death at Prague on 24 October 1601 — seven years past the deadline he had set himself, the opus still unassembled.
verdict.scholarly: Modern scholarship judges the failure not merely biographical. Kepler found the Mars orbit irreducible to either Ptolemaic theory or Tycho’s proposed geo-heliocentric replacement: an eight-arcminute residual remained that Tycho’s framework could not account for. Completing the opus required a physical, causal approach to planetary motion.
verdict.irony: That approach was Kepler’s own — and Tycho disapproved of it (Voelkel, The Composition of Kepler’s Astronomia Nova, Princeton 2001). The opus could only be finished by a method its author had rejected.

opus.afterlife: The pieces scattered after Tycho's death (Prague, 24 October 1601). Kepler completed the Progymnasmata from Tycho's unfinished sheets (Prague, 1602); Tengnagel sold the Mechanica woodblocks to Hülsius for a Nuremberg reprint (1602). The observation logs — the empirical core that would have filled the planetary Books III–VII — passed to Kepler under the Tengnagel–Kepler agreement of 8 July 1604 and fed the Astronomia Nova (1609) and the Rudolphine Tables (1627): Tycho's own title, but recast on the heliocentric-elliptical principles his whole geo-heliocentric programme existed to refute.

steps.text: Kepler completed the unfinished Progymnasmata from the 388 leaves printed at Uraniborg, adding 58 printed at Prague — 446 in all — and a closing appendix explaining the staged printing (Schumann press, Prague). Tycho's son-in-law Frans Gansneb Tengnagel sold the Mechanica woodblocks to Levinus Hülsius (Nuremberg), who had Christoph Lochner print the only commercial edition.

The Tengnagel–Kepler agreement (8 July 1604, mediated by Johannes Pistorius): Kepler receives all of Tycho's observation logs in exchange for completing the Rudolphine Tables “to Tengnagel's satisfaction.” The empirical core — everything that would have filled the planetary Books III–VII — now in Kepler's hands.

The logs yield the Astronomia Nova (1609) — the elliptical orbit and the equal-areas law. The Tabulae Rudolphinae follow (1627): Tycho's own title, honouring Rudolf II, but built on heliocentric-elliptical principles. Tycho himself had “negotiated a deal whereby he would publish his planetary theories under the name of the Rudolphine Tables and Kepler would help him” (Thoren) — the title he planned, the physics he rejected.

Ludwig Kepler sells the original observation autographs to Frederick III of Denmark (1655; now KB Copenhagen). The Vienna fair-copy transcripts pass to the Jesuit Albert Curtz (“Lucius Barrettus”), who prints the unreliable Historia Coelestis (Augsburg 1666; some sheets reissued Regensburg 1672). Erasmus Bartholin’s Specimen (1668) catalogued its errors.

Dreyer’s Opera Omnia (TBOO X–XIII, Copenhagen, 15 vols) publishes the observations in authoritative critical form — the data Tycho intended for Books III–VII, definitively edited 325 years after his death.

opus.source_line: Reconstructed from the primary documents (the 1592 Quaternio Primus, the 1588 Peucer letter, the Mechanica) and the biographies — Dreyer 1890, Thoren 1990, Christianson 2000 and 2020, Mosley 2007, Strano and Truffa; Voelkel 2001 for the Kepler verdict — all given in the Sources.

M_PROG_1602.description: The 388 leaves printed on Hven completed at Prague under Kepler's direction, at the press of Johann Schumann's heirs, with 58 new leaves: two preliminary quires )( and (:) (title, the heirs' dedication to Rudolf II of 31 July 1602, a preface, the privileges of Rudolf II and James VI, verses), the Moon section P⁸ Q⁸ R¹⁰ (paginated 01–028 and 113–136 to close the gap left in 1592), and the end Ggggg–Mmmmm (pp. 787–822: the Conclusio, Kepler's Appendix, index, errata) — 446 leaves in all. The new title: Typis inchoata Uraniburgi Daniae, absoluta Pragae Bohemiae, M.DC.II. The Moon quires mix Tycho's own type with Schumann's, never on one page (Nielsen 1921, pp. 209–210).

an engraved portrait (Strunk 356) pasted to the title-verso in some copies, a later copy of the 1592 woodcut

M_DEMUNDI_1603.description: The 1588 sheets, most of which had been held back to be issued with the first volume, issued at Prague by the heirs in 1603 with two new preliminary quires in place of the original ✱⁴ (title; Tengnagel's dedication to the imperial secretary Johannes Barvitius; a preface to the reader; Tycho's old preface) and the last two leaves (Nnn) reprinted; 242 leaves for 238. Printed at the Schumann press with very little of Tycho's own material; the Chemistry emblem on the last leaf and the colophon Pragae Bohemorum, absolvebatur typis Schumanianis, M.DC.III (Nielsen 1921, p. 211).
M_DEMUNDI_1603.census_inclusion: the De mundi census counts 1588 sheets only; the re-issues are not censused

M_EPIST_1602.description: Immediately after Tycho's death the heirs sold the stock of the Epistolae to the Nuremberg bookseller Levinus Hülsius, who had a new title-quire printed — the title with Noribergae apud Levinum Hulsium … anno MDCI (a misprint for 1602), the rest of the quire a reprint of the old — and issued the book the same year; the old colophon retained. The material is Christoph Lochner's (Nielsen 1921, pp. 211–212).
M_EPIST_1602.census_inclusion: counted in the Epistolae census as an issue-state of the one impression

M_MECH_1602.description: A new edition in a wholly new setting, printed for Hülsius at Nuremberg in 1602 from Tycho's original woodblocks and copperplates. Hülsius was a publisher, not a printer; the material assigns the book, like the Epistolae title-quire, to Christoph Lochner. Libraries catalogue it as 1598 when the title-leaf is wanting (Nielsen 1921, p. 212).

M_PROG_1610.description: After Hülsius's death the remaining stock of all three books passed to the Frankfurt bookseller Gottfried Tampach, who issued them in 1610 with new titles and some parts reprinted. For the Progymnasmata the title-quire was reprinted (the title, partly in red: … Excudi primum caepta Uraniburgi Daniae, ast Pragae Bohemiae absoluta. Prostant Francofurti apud Godefridum Tampachium, M.DCX), and in some copies quires B and C (pp. 9–24), in most quires Kk and Ll (fol. 257–272, the first two quires of the star catalogue). The reason is an undated stocktake on a loose leaf in Cod. Vindob. lat. 10688: 1,197 copies of the first part in all, 400 sent to Frankfurt, at least 150 copies of quire B and 50 of quire C to be reprinted, some 200 copies imperfect. The publisher's device is one Matthias Becker used in books of the same year, so Becker may have printed the supplements (Nielsen 1921, pp. 212–213 and n. 1).

states.label: quires B and C reset (some copies); quires Kk and Ll reset (most copies)

M_DEMUNDI_1610.description: Tampach had the two preliminary quires reprinted after the Prague issue of 1603, only the title changed (… Excudi primum caeptus Uraniburgi Daniae, ast Pragae Bohemiae absolutus. Prostat Francofurti apud Godefridum Tampachium, M.DCX); no new colophon. Copies carry either the original final quire of 1588 or the 1603 one — which led Bibliotheca Danica (II, p. 77) to list two differently made-up copies as two editions (Nielsen 1921, p. 213 and n. 2).

With these issues the Uraniborg stock was at last used up; the Frankfurt edition of 1648 is new print from first to last (Nielsen 1921, pp. 213–214).

printed_not_preserved.basis: Tycho to Scultetus, 7 January 1600; Nielsen suspects the scrapped sheets served the Prague compositors as copy-text (1921, pp. 207, 210)

printed_not_preserved.what: The Progymnasmata Moon section, second printing
printed_not_preserved.extent: begun on Hven paper fetched from the Wandsbek store, now reckoned at six quires instead of three; halted when the lunar eclipse of January 1599 disagreed with the tables; abandoned at the departure for Prague after Easter
printed_not_preserved.basis: Tycho to Hagecius, 26 February 1599; Tycho to Longomontanus, 21 March 1599 (Nielsen 1921, p. 208)

chronology_events.event: Tycho to Anders Sørensen Vedel: he will set up a small press at Uraniborg and buy type at the coming Frankfurt fair.
The printer Joachim engaged and sent to Wittenberg for presses and type; further type brokered through Heinrich Brucaeus and the Rostock printer Stephan Möllmann, December 1584 to April 1585.
The Ulfeldt poem dated at Uraniborg (7 Kal. Decemb.); with the Pratensis epitaph the earliest prints of the press, followed the same season by the poems to Gjøe and Lange.
Tycho's letter announcing the little astrological calendar for the year — the Diarium — planned in 2,000 copies.
The Rantzau poem dated; it names the Orthographia, the woodcut plan of Uraniborg, among the small prints finished early in 1585.
Tycho to Hagecius: the manuscript of the astronomical work ready for the press, paper awaited from abroad; an imperial privilege requested.
Paper arrives; the printing of the De mundi begins, the second tome first.
Tycho to Heinrich von Below: paper sought from the Duke of Mecklenburg's mills.
'Finis I lib.' in the meteorological diary: the De mundi finished.
The paper mill on Hven working from 1589/90; its two watermarks identify island paper.
Tycho to Vedel: the printing has come to a standstill this autumn; the printer sent to Germany for paper and a paper-maker.
Flemløs's Astrologia leaves the press in Danish; the German edition follows in September.
Advance copies of the Progymnasmata title-quire sent: three to the Landgrave of Hesse (20 February), three to Hugo Blotius (20 March), six to Hagecius (22 March).
Tycho to Rantzau: the second volume of the Epistolae in the press.
Tycho leaves Hven with press and instruments (the Loca register's date; Nielsen gives 29 April).
Arrival at Wandsbek, Rantzau's castle near Hamburg; the press set up with Philip de Ohr's type.
The Mechanica issued, its dedication to Rudolf II dated 31 December 1597.
Tycho leaves Wandsbek in the autumn; the Moon section printed at Hamburg under Longomontanus's eye is scrapped.
Winter at Wittenberg on account of the plague at Prague; the Moon section begun again on Hven paper, and abandoned after Easter 1599.
Tycho to Scultetus from Prague: the first quire and the Conclusio unprinted, the Moon section wanting, the press still at Magdeburg; the state of every book set out.
The press reaches Prague.
Tycho dies at Prague; the whole manuscript ready, the printing finished under Kepler.
The Progymnasmata completed at Prague (the heirs' dedication of 31 July); the Epistolae stock sold to Hülsius and re-issued at Nuremberg; the Mechanica reprinted there by Lochner.
The De mundi re-issued at Prague with new preliminaries.
Tampach re-issues all three books at Frankfurt; the Uraniborg stock used up.
A new Frankfurt edition of the works, new print from first to last: the end of Nielsen's story.

desiderata.title: The Mechanica's collation in the Dansk Bibliografi
desiderata.text: The formula in DB 432 as transcribed for this edition — ):(:(⁴ A⁴ B⁴–F⁴ G⁸ H⁴ — sums to 40 leaves against the 42 the entry states; Nielsen 1921 (p. 205) gives ):(⁴ A⁶ B⁴–F⁴ G⁶ H⁶, which sums, and is followed here. Whether the DB entry itself or the house transcription carries the error should be checked on the page image.

desiderata.title: The Apologia's witnesses
desiderata.text: The Berlin fragment copied from the 1591 print (prefaced by Craig's three letters) is most likely a war loss; its shelfmark and the Kraków alternative are unresolved. The Kepler-papers copy identified by Norlind as Pulkovo MSS vol. 19, fols 115–150 (St Petersburg) and the Longomontanus–From manuscript named by Gassendi are untraced. Any of them would carry the 1591 text; only the Berlin fragment could show the print's own setting.

desiderata.title: Tycho's working copy of the Progymnasmata (Königsberg)
desiderata.text: Given by Tycho to Johannes Müller in March 1598, corrected throughout in his hand, with twelve blank leaves bound in where the Moon section was pending; last at the Staats- und Universitätsbibliothek Königsberg, untraced since the dispersal of 1944–45. It is the one witness that could fix the boundary between what was printed on Hven and what was completed at Prague. The Königsberg holdings now at Toruń, Olsztyn, Vilnius and Kaliningrad have not been asked.

desiderata.title: Five posthumous issues without a census
desiderata.text: De mundi 1603 and 1610, Epistolae 1602 and 1610, Progymnasmata 1610 are described here from Nielsen but have no copy-by-copy census; the Epistolae issues are counted inside the 1596 census as issue-states, the De mundi issues excluded from theirs by rule, the Progymnasmata 1610 nowhere. Tampach's stocktake of 1,197 copies suggests the Frankfurt issues survive in numbers; Nielsen calls them common. A census of each would complete the copy layer.

desiderata.title: Four printings of which nothing is preserved
desiderata.text: The second volume of the Epistolae (about 50 leaves printed, 1597), the third tome of the Progymnasmata (begun 1590), and the two printings of the Moon section (Hamburg 1598, scrapped; Wittenberg 1599, abandoned) are entered under the presses (§6) on Nielsen's authority and not as editions. Should a sheet of any of them be identified — in a binding, as printer's waste, as the Prague compositors' copy — it would become an edition row.

desiderata.title: The inserted leaf in the Prague University copy of the Epistolae
desiderata.text: Nielsen (1921, p. 201 n. 4) records in the Prague University Library copy an inserted leaf 'Tabulae conversionum graduum …' marked 'Post fol. 108', not printed at Uraniborg. No house store records it; the copy's census entry should.

desiderata.title: The Icones states copy by copy
desiderata.text: The Vienna copy of the 1596 album has a reset title-leaf and a printed afterword not printed at Uraniborg (Nielsen: most likely by de Ohr at Hamburg, early 1598); the Wrocław copy has the afterword copied in by hand on Bl. 11a. The census records the states in prose; a state field per copy would let the table show them.

desiderata.title: Was the Lange poem the first thing printed at Uraniborg?
desiderata.text: A note in the shared thesaurus claimed that Tycho's diary records the Lange poem as the first print of the press (27 November 1584). The printed Diarium carries no such entry, Nielsen names the Pratensis epitaph as probably the earliest print, and the Ulfeldt poem carries the earliest date (25 November 1584). The claim is marked unverified until a source is produced.

desiderata.title: Five copy records to disposition in the censuses
desiderata.text: The retired hand-picked copy list carried five records the censuses do not hold or hold differently: a Mechanica 1598 at Prague under the shelfmark AG XI 56 (the Strahov Hasenburg copy is Hasselberg 23); the Pruskovský copy placed at Křivoklát where the census has the Národní muzeum; a Copenhagen 1592 Progymnasmata title-leaf; a De mundi 1603 at the Library of Congress; three Epistolae 1610 at the Royal Danish Library. Each is filed as a census proposal, not silently dropped.

desiderata.title: Concordance numbers not yet entered
desiderata.text: Houzeau and Lancaster's numbers, Bibliotheca Danica's entries and the VD16 numbers for the German-printed issues are not yet in the concordance (§5); Norman's number is entered for the 1602 Mechanica only.
